identity.title: Genome Editing of Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Neurological Disease: Progress and Translational Barriers.

content.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a shared mechanism across neurological disease. Specifically, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial DNA damage are factors in primary mitochondrial disorders and major neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson, Alzheimer, and Huntington diseases, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. This review surveys the mechanisms driving mitochondrial dysfunction and evaluates the current landscape of gene-editing technologies developed to address them. We examine mitochondria-targeted editors and nuclear-targeted editors, examining the editing capability, delivery constraints, and off-target risk of each. Heteroplasmy-shifting nucleases currently offer the strongest in vivo evidence for mtDNA-directed therapy, while base editors extend correction to homoplasmic mutations at the cost of a narrower editing scope and off-target editing. Nuclear editing platforms avoid the mitochondrial gRNA import barrier entirely, allowing current technologies to achieve the most progress toward functional, behavioral rescue in animal models. Across all platforms, delivery efficiency, off-target specificity, and translation from rodent to primate models remain unresolved barriers to clinical application. Gene editing for mitochondrial dysfunction is highly creditable as a precision therapy for genetically defined disease subsets, including primary mitochondrial disease and other neurodegenerative disorders with a known nuclear driver, rather than as a universal strategy for sporadic neurodegeneration, where mitochondrial dysfunction arises from multifactorial and poorly localized causes.
